🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.26% (intraday, 7-year -4bp). At trading day 28 (last close) it was +0.35% against a five-campaign average of -1.20% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.77%. The 10-year is -3bp since the hike vs a +18bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 804bp against a five-year average of 415bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +33bp and BB +24bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.33 → 0.62 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+8bp).
  • Bank Earnings: 1 bank reported (CBU); 1 red-flagged (CBU: NPLs +22% QoQ). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: CBU.
  • Stocks: Stocks rose, led by tech; the Nasdaq gained more than one percent.
  • FX: The dollar index rose a little; the euro stayed well below its recent average.
  • Technicals: The S&P is just above its short-term trend line; history suggests a turn is possible.
  • Sectors: Tech and shopping stocks led; energy, staples and property stocks lagged.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lending to most companies stays cheap, but loans to the weakest borrowers keep getting dearer.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; the main risk is the weakest corporate borrowers.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady, not falling fast, and energy keeps prices sticky.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices look stretched in places, but are far from the 2000 mania.
  • Earnings & IPOs: We watch Apple (largest company) and Super Micro (most volatile); this week's US IPOs are unconfirmed.
  • Iran: We couldn't confirm any October Iran news; oil near $100 shows the risk remains.
  • Warsh: Warsh's Fed leans hawkish; a hike was expected in September, but that's unconfirmed.
  • Week Ahead: The Fed decision, Amazon and Apple earnings, factory data and the jobs report.
  • Outlook: Neutral short term: stocks are strong, but trouble is growing among the weakest borrowers.
  • Trades: Stay long stocks with tight stops, reduce weak junk bonds, and stay short the euro.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 3 buy, 1 sell, 18 hold long, 23 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 6.2% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads calm
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.58 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 91th pctile, +30bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Oil Model: WTI $101.76 (2026-10-26). Oil model Base $104 / $93 / $83 at 3/6/12 months (Bull $99, Bear $67 at 12m), probability-weighted $83, against a futures strip of $99 / $93 / $83. Growth leadership returned in the PM session. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.18% to 26,477.81, the Russell 2000 gained 1.16% to 2,818.87 and the S&P 500 added 0.60% to 7,722.60. The Dow was flat (+0.03%) and the VIX eased from 18.39 to 17.52. Info Tech (+1.49%) and Cons Discretionary (+1.36%) led, while Energy (-2.20%) fell as WTI dropped 1.83% to 99.9 and Brent fell 1.51% to 114.06. Abroad the Nikkei rose 1.73% and the Euro Stoxx 50 0.79%, but the FTSE 100 fell 0.75%. Treasuries sold off slightly at the front end, with the 2Y at 4.7369% (+2.1bp) and the 10Y at 4.9967%. The biggest story is still beneath the surface in junk credit. In the hy_contagion data (as of 2026-10-26) the Caa–B gap is 804bp, more than double its 830bp... correction: well above its 5-year average of about 415bp. That is the 100th percentile of the last five years and the widest since 2020-04-15. Caa spreads are up 150bp in a month and 278bp in three months. The FRED ICE CCC–B gap (1,013bp, as of 2026-10-23) confirms the move. Is the CCC stress spreading upward? Partly, but not decisively. Single-B is up 33bp in one month and Ba is up 24bp, yet both tightened over the past week (B -8bp, Ba -1bp). The B–Ba gap of 117bp sits below its 5-year average, and IG is only 88bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.62 from 0.33 three months ago but is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. Contagion is building at the bottom of the ladder but has not yet clearly broken into BB or IG. These are descriptive readings, not a validated signal. Sentiment is constructive but late-cycle, with an FOMC decision reportedly due on Oct 28 under Chair Warsh and megacap earnings ahead.

“Tech is still running, but the junk-bond basement is filling with water. Watch whether it reaches the B and BB floors before you add more risk.”
📊Markets

US equities closed higher, but breadth varied by style. The S&P 500 gained 0.60% (+45.83) to 7,722.60 and the Nasdaq Composite 1.18% (+308.43) to 26,477.81. The Russell 2000 matched it with +1.16% to 2,818.87, while the Dow added only 0.03% to 52,377.57. The VIX fell 4.73% to 17.52. In Europe the Euro Stoxx 50 rose 0.79% to 6,164.69 and the STOXX 600 0.47% to 643.68, but the FTSE 100 lost 0.75% to 10,686.54, likely on its energy weighting as crude slid. The Nikkei 225 jumped 1.73% to 63,268.37. Rates edged higher in the US: the 2Y was 4.7369%, the 10Y 4.9967% and the 30Y 5.3103%. The Bund 10Y slipped to 3.36%, the JGB 10Y rose to 2.813% and the Gilt 10Y held at 5.346%. In commodities, WTI fell 1.83% to 99.9 and Brent 1.51% to 114.06. Copper rose 1.69% to 665.25, natural gas jumped 3.65% to 2.697 and gold was flat at 4,062.02.

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil (Europe/Asia Diesel) — current: 1444.50 $/tonne vs Brent

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil is pinned at $1444.5/tonne, at the 99.7th percentile of its history (z 3.1), and every gauge of tightness is at an extreme too: the crack against Brent is at $79.6826/bbl (z 5.6), and the curve is in steep backwardation, with front-minus-12th at $382.75 and front-minus-36th at $655.0. The market is paying a large premium for prompt middle distillate supply and heavily discounting the deferred months, which is typical of an acute supply squeeze. Every card's history of similar extremes points lower, but the very wide stops show that squeezes like this can run much further before they break, so position size matters more than direction.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

The Caa–B gap is 804bp, at the 100th percentile of five years and the widest since 2020-04-15. Single-B is 314bp (+33bp in 1m) and Ba is 197bp (+24bp in 1m), both near the median of five years. IG at 0.88 is near its historic floor (hist min 0.71). A move above 1.00 would mean contagion had reached investment grade. On the downside, HY back toward 3.00 would need Caa to stabilize. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.58 vol points (19th percentile of the 53 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 97.9 (70th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 86bp (flatter by 4bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (116bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 26 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The rhyme with 2000 is in credit and volatility, not in prices. Since its Oct-2022 anchor the current Nasdaq path has reached 241.0 after 48 months. On the computed chart, the 1990-anchored dot-com path stood at 235.7 by month 48 and went on to peak at month 113, while the 1994-anchored path peaked at month 69. On that analog, today looks mid-cycle rather than terminal. The bigger vulnerabilities are elsewhere. Index concentration is at a historic high (analyst estimate ~40% top-10 weight, vs roughly 25% in 2000), so a stumble by a few megacaps would move the whole index. Market-cap-to-GDP (~210%, analyst estimate) and CAPE (~38x, analyst estimate) are near or above 2000 levels, even though trailing tech P/Es are not. What would turn this into a 2000 setup: an inverted curve, ISM rolling over from 54–55, and a surge in IPO issuance and margin debt. None is in place yet. The five figures supplied here are analyst estimates that could not be verified by web search this session; treat them as approximate.

⚔️Iran War

We could not verify any developments dated October 2026; search returned only February–May 2026 coverage. Verified background: the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28, 2026, starting a weekslong war that spread regionally. A ceasefire followed. By May, Trump said he had extended it until Tehran submitted a proposal to end the war, while Iran accused the US of a 'grave violation' and Secretary Rubio said a deal was still possible. Iran was also reported attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and France deployed a carrier group toward the Red Sea. The market read: Brent at 114.06 and WTI at 99.9 point to a large energy risk premium still embedded in prices, whatever the diplomatic status.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: a hold or a 25bp hike at the next meeting (reportedly Oct 28), with a hawkish bias. Verified facts: in June, Warsh's first meeting as chair, the Fed held unanimously at 3.50–3.75%, and the median dot rose to 3.8% for year-end. A September preview put futures at 92% odds of a hike to 3.75–4.00%. We could not confirm the September outcome. The 2Y at 4.7369% is consistent with the market pricing further tightening (analyst inference).

~1 YEAR

Inference: policy stays restrictive over about a year. Warsh's long-standing record criticizes an oversized Fed balance sheet and favors 'regime change' at the Fed, which points to continued balance-sheet shrinkage plus data-driven rates. Cuts would likely wait until energy-driven inflation (Flexible CPI 6.12%) fades. This is inferred from his prior positions; this session's search did not surface new speeches.

Reports from Warsh's debut described the Fed as data-driven under him. They flagged that the Board, not the chair alone, is the signal. Energy-driven inflation from the Iran war (CPI cited at 4.2% YoY in May) pushed the committee toward tightening, while a reported US–Iran agreement trimmed some hike bets. With core PCE at 3.00759% and payroll growth weak (29k), Warsh faces a stagflation-tinged trade-off. Expect hawkish rhetoric on inflation credibility, with the balance sheet as his preferred lever. The specifics of the October meeting are unverified.
